name: Pidgin Hamer
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog lists only Petrollino 2016 'Language variation and patterns of language use' (doctype: minimal); no description of the pidgin's phonology exists

sources.citation: Petrollino, Sara. 2019. Between tone and stress in Hamar. In Clem, Jenks & Sande (eds.), Theory and description in African Linguistics (ACAL 47), 287-302. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3367150.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Word-prosody of Hamar proper (hame1242) only: lexically contrastive accent in nouns, grammatical accent in verbs. No mention of the pidgin, contact variety or non-native speech (a full-text search for stress/accent pidgin/contact/L2: none).

sources.citation: Petrollino, Sara. 2016. A grammar of Hamar: a South Omotic language of Ethiopia. PhD dissertation, Leiden University / Université Lumière Lyon 2 (hdl.handle.net/1887/44090; theses.fr 2016LYSE2176); printed as Cushitic and Omotic Studies 6, Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. Section 1.1.2 'Language variation and patterns of language use', pp. 2-4 (= Glottolog ref 551488, the only reference Glottolog lists for pidg1260).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Ch. 2 (2.4 Word prosody, pp. 40-42) describes stress and tone of Hamar proper only (lexical, unpredictable stress in nouns). The pidgin is treated solely in the sociolinguistic note 1.1.2 (pp. 3-4): the only phonological remark is 'The ʻpidgin Hamarʼ shows a high degree of phonological convergence with Amharic' (p. 4); nothing on stress, accent or tone of the pidgin anywhere in the 368-page text (a full-text search for stress/accent: pp. 3-4, p. 12 fieldwork note, CV).

sources.citation: Petrollino, Sara. 2023. Hamar. In Ronny Meyer, Zelealem Leyew & Bedilu Wakjira (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Ethiopian Languages, 948-972. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

sources.note: The only other primary source that mentions the pidgin: p. 397 coins the label 'pidgin Hamer' (per Petrollino 2016:3). It is the one place a pre-2016 remark on how outsiders pronounce Hamar might exist; it also contains Lydall's original account of Hamar stress/tone.

sources.note: Petrollino 2016:4 notes that verb forms in this Italian-era wordlist carry a formative -inden resembling the pidgin's invariant -índane, i.e. the wordlist may itself record pidginised Hamar; any accent marks in it would be the only early prosodic evidence.
